title: The Three Dwellings: how the Living Spirit stripped the archons of water, darkness, and fire
arc: The teaching opens with the question of how three corrupt dwellings were poured out of heaven and separated forth from the archons; it answers by likening the Living Spirit to a wise physician who applies three medicines and to a Youth wearing garments in the womb, then enumerates twelve works of the resulting cosmic economy by which the dripping of darkness is bound in strongholds around the worlds and the heavens are kept pure until the consummation.
reading:
This chapter answers a single doctrinal question: how were the three "dwellings of deceit" — those of water, of darkness, and of fire — drawn out from all the archons above and separated forth so that the heavens could stand pure? The teaching insists that we must "recognize" how this pouring-out happened, because the entire economy of the cosmos rests on it. What is being described, in correspondential terms, is the Lord's work of extracting the three modes of falsity hidden in the natural heavens (corrupted truth, falsity-from-evil, and the burning of self-love) and binding them in fixed strongholds outside the redemptive arena, so that good can grow in the natural without being instantly overwhelmed.

The first analogy frames the whole operation: the archons, full of these three poisons, are like a single sick man whose body holds many diseases — gall, plagues, hidden venoms in the inner members. A wise physician does not attack everything at once. He prepares one antidote against the taste of the disease, another purgative for the lower place, another medicine to soothe the blows; he works in stillness and silence, with the τέχνη of his beautiful consuming medicines, "uprooting the hidden one at the end" by the very scent of the cure. The Living Spirit is this wise physician, and the three dwellings of water, darkness, and fire are his three medicines — the very disorder, once isolated and externalized, becomes the means of the cosmos's healing.

The second figure deepens this. The three are also "the three garments that the Living Spirit wears upon his body": wind, water, and fire — that is, perception, truth in the natural, and the active power of love — which he establishes within the works that are below. By putting these on he revealed himself forth to the archons "in single-mindedness, with trembling, in an expulsion forth," and so poured out from them the three places of deceit. The Spirit clothes himself in the very elements of the natural in order to draw their corrupt counterparts out into the open.

A third image — the Youth in his mother's womb — explains how the Spirit's "teaching" (ⲧⲥⲃⲱ) is structured. The child wears seven garments in succession: marrow, bone, sinew, flesh, vein, bond, and skin — the full anatomy of structural good, framework, communicating power, natural concupiscence, channels of truth, binding, and outermost ultimate. When the Youth's own giving is added, these "are perfected and become eight teachings," the eighth being the new state beyond the seven of natural completion. The soul of the Youth dwells within all these, encompassed by them; and at the moment when the scent of the demon's energies in the bond of offspring is revealed, the Youth comes forth out of their action without wound or blow. The point is the change of "thought" by which the soul passes from being clothed in the womb-garments of mingled state into the new garment. So also the strongholds of Mother, Darkness, and Fire — the energies that belonged to the Youth — are made like him and revealed; the third Living teaching of the Spirit is precisely this. In the likeness of the teaching of the Mother (the corrupt matrix, here the Hyle-pole) the Spirit drove down all the shadow of destruction with its mire and bound it in the stronghold of Darkness which encircles the cosmos. In the likeness of the teaching of the Living Fire, the burning of the archons in their hardness was poured out, cast onto the earth, drawn back from the earth, and bound in the stronghold which encircles all the worlds — what is called the Wall of the Great Fire. The work was not done all at once but each one in its own proper season.

The teaching then argues counterfactually why this stripping had to be done. Had the dripping of darkness and the fire never been driven down from the heavens to earth, then forced out from earth and shut up in the encircling river-wall, concupiscence would have continued raising itself up in trees and fruits and every flesh; the power of fire and the burning of self-love now distributed across ten thousand men of today would have been concentrated in a single man, and no one would have been able to grasp truth or hold thought or knowledge. Multiplied falsity, sealed inside the natural, would have made regeneration impossible. The whole present cosmos is therefore an arrangement made possible by the Living Spirit's prior act of separating forth and binding.

From this one stripping the chapter then unfolds twelve great works that constitute the cosmic economy. The First is the driving-out itself, scattering the dwellings from heaven to earth and then concealing them outside, to the sides of the worlds, to the other region of the Zone — so that evil "may not abound in the cosmos, neither in the creatures, nor in the trees." The Second purifies the heavens and firmaments themselves of defilement. The Third concerns Error, who would otherwise be unrestrained. The Fourth purifies the place of harvest. The Fifth concerns the wealth that dwells in the ships of light, in which there is nothing chosen and holy that is not refined. The Sixth: the temples of the upper place are united, completed, at rest, pure, with no rest that fails or is weak among them. The Seventh: the archons sprout themselves at the rivers that give forth light, and arrive at their proper places and regions. The Eighth: great fashionings and preparations close up all the works. The Ninth: when the apostles are sent to the world they give the sign at the head of the dissolution of the world. The Tenth: they become releasers and purifiers of all works to the end of the cosmos, in the manner of the fire that shall fall. The Eleventh: the archons with their entire host are banished to the country that is outside, because they begrudge "this honored one who is a rich man beyond them" — the Aeons of Light that exist outside, the place of peace, honor, mercy, where the joy of the inhabitants neither passes nor departs. The Twelfth: all the works of the Half-region, hidden away from the Aeons of Light, of the lineage of the Wall of Fire that surrounds the whole structure, are set down and made manifest within their boundary.

These twelve are the complete circuit (twelve = completeness in church / all aspects) of the divine economy that follows from the original three-fold extraction. The "mighty ones who ate" — the archons gorged on the Living Soul — were banished not only to the earth but to the further place of binding, and over them "the three words of Life keep watch," set upon their feet in a great might, that they may keep guard at the time of the end.

Read whole, the teaching is therefore an exposition of how the Lord, in his operative power as Living Spirit, performs a triple discrimination upon the natural heavens: he draws out the corrupt water (mingled truth), the darkness (falsity-from-evil), and the fire (burning of self-love), clothes himself in their pure correspondents (wind, water, fire as garments of perception, truth, love), and binds the corrupt three in encircling strongholds — the Wall of Great Fire being the outermost. Inside that wall the twelvefold economy then unfolds, in which apostles, ships, temples, harvests, and rivers all do their refining work, until at the consummation the archons are sealed in their outer country and the three Words of Life stand watch over them forever. The whole arc moves from physician's diagnosis, through the Spirit's clothing-himself in the elements, to the established cosmic order in which redemption can actually take place.
